newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FOCUS-Waigel firm as French put budget pact on hold.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel firm as French put budget pact on hold.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, architect of the stability pact whose fate was thrown into confusion on Monday, warned that Bonn would not allow any softening of the deal seen as crucial to German acceptance of European economic and monetary union.
"There will be no change of our policy," Waigel stated flatly at a news conference during a meeting of EU finance ministers here.

The finance minister of France's newly elected Socialist-led government, Dominique Strauss-Kahn, on Monday told his EU counterparts that France would not be able to state its position on the pact before Prime Minister Lionel Jospin makes his first address to parliament on June 19.
Strauss-Kahn said France wanted to add a protocol to the stability pact to reinforce EMU coordination on growth and job creation measures.

The move means that the pact Waigel fought so hard for in a bid to enforce fiscal discipline among euro-zone members after the launch of the single currency cannot now be formally ratified at a summit of EU leaders in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.

The stability and growth pact, agreed after tough negotiations at an EU summit in Dublin last December, imposes sanctions on countries exceeding the budget deficit limit of three percent of gross domestic product after the launch of the single currency, scheduled to start on January 1, 1999.

The pact, always regarded as essential to dispelling German fears that the planned single currency will not be as stable as the mark, has gained even greater significance recently amid growing fears that monetary union, if it is launched on time, may result in a soft currency.
Seeking to dispel the impression of an EU rift, Waigel said France's EU partners were sympathetic to the new French government's need for more time to consider its position on the pact.
"But delegates also expressed clearly that the pact as it has been agreed is not open for negotiation," Waigel said.
He noted that Strauss-Kahn had not asked for a renegotiation of the pact but was considering adding elements to it which would place greater emphasis on job creation.
Waigel reiterated that Germany believed employment schemes should remain the preserve of national decision-making but added Bonn was ready to discuss any French proposals.
"Whether there can be any additions will be decided by discussions in the next few weeks," Waigel said.

He warned that it was important for the sake of avoiding upsetting financial markets to achieve final polictical ratification of the stability pact, the EMS II mechanism linking non euro zone currencies to the planned euro, and of the legal framework for monetary union.
EU sources said the inability to ratify the stability pact in Amsterdam may delay final approval of EU reforms at the summit.
A senior source close to the German delegation said he was confident the stability pact would be formally ratified by the end of June, once France had made its position clear.
But the source, who declined to be named, also made clear that there was a limit to how far Bonn would go on the issue of adding employment policy to the pact.
"We agree we have to coordinate better on economic and financial policies but we are against an economic government which would affect the independence of a European central bank."

The source also said Waigel had not been questioned by his EU counterparts about his failed plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves this year in a bid to plug Bonn's gaping deficit and enable it to qualify for monetary union.

Germany looks increasingly unlikely to meet the three percent deficit criterion for monetary union and Waigel continues to state that countries will not be able to join with a deficit above three percent.
He reiterated that position on Monday, ruling out that a deficit of 3.3 percent would be sufficient.

Allowing a country to join monetary union with such a deficit, as advocated by a senior German banker at the weekend, would pave the way for other nations to join with even higher deficit overshoots, Waigel told reporters.
There is only one figure in the treaty and that is three," he said.
